source.citation: Albert A. Bell, Jr., An Historiographical Analysis of the De Excidio Hierosolymitano of Pseudo-Hegesippus (1977)
source.numbering: Ussani DEH paragraph and Niese Josephus section. Longer intervals are limited to the locations that correspond.

targets.note: Mattathias refuses the king’s orders and kills the man who sacrifices.
Ptolemy kills Simon at a banquet. The accounts differ over the fate of Simon’s sons.
Compare the account of Antiochus’s Parthian campaign and the use of “Medes” in DEH and BJ.
Twelve thousand Jews are killed. Few Romans die and more are wounded.
Pompey sees the sacred vessels and leaves the Temple treasure untouched. Bell proposes a common source for the similarities.
Scaurus attacks Petra and withdraws after Aretas agrees to pay him three hundred talents.
After Pompey’s death, Antipater aligns himself with Caesar.
Antigonus brings his family’s grievances before Caesar.
Antipater defends himself by recalling what he did for Caesar in Egypt.
Caesar confirms Hyrcanus as high priest, appoints Antipater procurator, and authorizes rebuilding the walls.
Pacorus and Barzapharnes intervene on behalf of Antigonus. Bell notes DEH’s explanation that rebellions detained Pacorus.
Herod returns from his wedding and the armies gather before Jerusalem.
Sosius joins Herod at Jerusalem at Antony’s command.
Jerusalem is taken, its inhabitants are killed, and Antigonus surrenders to Sosius.
Herod protects the Temple and promises to pay the Roman troops from his own funds.
Sosius offers a crown and takes Antigonus to Antony. The accounts give different explanations of his execution.
Josephus gives Herod a different speech before the battle with the Arabs.
Herod meets Octavian at Rhodes and defends his loyalty to Antony.
Octavian accepts Herod’s defence and asks for the loyalty he showed Antony.
Octavian restores Herod’s diadem, and Herod accompanies him on his way to Egypt.
Herod builds a harbour larger than Piraeus and provides safe inner anchorages.
Tryphon the barber reports that Tiro offered him a reward in Alexander’s name for killing Herod.
At the hearing before Varus, a letter from Antipater’s mother is read and Antipater begs to be heard.
Herod accuses Antipater of plotting against him and recalls Antipater’s accusations against his brothers.
Herod breaks off and Antipater defends himself, questioning evidence obtained under torture.
Antipater’s speech moves the audience. Josephus also depicts Herod as moved and hiding his feelings.
The pretender’s resemblance to Alexander brings him gifts. The routes described differ.
Josephus gives a different account of Herod’s motive for imprisoning and executing John the Baptist.
The governor suspects revolt and sends cavalry and infantry to kill the people who had gone out.
The account ends with the Jews interpreting Herod’s defeat as punishment for John’s death.
The thirteen high priests from Moses to Solomon and the succession to their office.
Pompey sends Aristobulus to Rome and restores Hyrcanus to the high priesthood without a diadem.
Antigonus reigns for three years and three months before Herod replaces him.
Vespasian sees the opportunity to capture Josephus at Jotapata and end the war.
The woman reveals Josephus’s hiding place, and Vespasian sends Paulinus and Gallicanus.
Vespasian sends Nicanor, who had been a friend of Josephus.
The priest Ananias, the scribe Aristeus, and fifteen other prominent people are killed.
Titus gathers his bravest soldiers to encourage them to attack.
Titus invokes Josephus when recalling how Jeconiah surrendered to spare Jerusalem.
The Romans raise siege banks against the Temple. DEH describes the preparations earlier in its account.

Latin.note: The Latin starts with Mathathias' refusal. The preliminary Greek promise of public example and royal honour is compressed in this transcription. The surviving refusal and its continuation are retained.
The killings and Roman resentment survive. Latin names Herod directly where Greek refers to the Jewish force around Herod; no subject is supplied or rewritten.
The weak/strong contrast survives; Greek’s initial rhetorical question about deeming the enemy brave is not separately expressed in this Latin interval.
Continued loyalty and counsel survive; the Latin does not separately name Cleopatra or expressly state the killing counsel here. The following interval begins with its counterfactual result.
Restoration of the diadem and honours survive. The Latin recasts Caesar’s letter and does not independently express the Greek gladiator-assistance notice.

Earliest surviving local narrative is the council's reaction, matching Greek epi toutois inside 106; the preceding offer to undergo torture is not separately narrated in this Latin context. Preserve the existing independent traditional Greek start at offset 35 and qualify partial correspondence. The later rhetorical offer in 119 is not silently moved into 106.
